strengths: The paper makes a clear conceptual contribution: it connects biophysically-grounded ATP consumption to a tractable Fisher-information-based optimal coding framework, which prior work (Ganguli & Simoncelli, Wang et al., Wang et al. 2016 metabolic constraints) has not done, and it explains the tuning-curve flattening observed empirically under caloric deprivation that existing models capture only partially.

The analytical results are convincing and well-organized: the framework recovers the mean firing rate constraint, population size constraint, and total-FI constraint of prior models as special cases (α=1, α=3/2), with a proposition (App. E) showing homeostasis emerges as a signature of optimality in Ganguli & Simoncelli's framework; solutions are derived for infomax, discrimax, and general Lp objectives (Tab. 1, Apps. D, K).

The biophysical simulation (NEURON, 10,000 trials per parameter state, detailed parameter tables in App. G) provides a principled grounding for the two free elements of the theory (α and the dispersed Poisson noise factor ηκ(E)), yielding a concrete, testable noise-energy trade-off (eq. 18-19) and predictions about resting potential/leak conductance relationships that are measurable with patch-clamp experiments.

Reproducibility is relatively strong: full simulation parameters, energy accounting details, fitting procedures (with reported relative error bounds <2%), and the simulation code are provided; robustness to non-uniform priors and homeostatic deviations across objectives are analyzed in App. L.

The writing is clear and the figure 1 unification diagram effectively communicates how the new framework generalizes prior work; the distinction between widening (Gabor-preserving) vs. flattening tuning curve changes is a genuinely useful modeling insight (footnote 1).
weaknesses: The empirical validation is thin and partly circular: the key data comparison (Sec. 5) fixes a single free parameter (a2/(a1·ϵctr) = 0.19625) specifically so the model reproduces the reported 32% widening and 29% ATP reduction from the single dataset of [22]; the model is fit to the phenomenon it claims to predict rather than tested on held-out predictions, and no independent dataset is used.

The central biophysical assumption — that cells adapt along an optimal path minimizing noise at every energy budget (eq. 15) — is asserted rather than derived or independently validated; it is the linchpin connecting simulation to theory, and its justification is essentially 'it produces the desired answer'.

Several approximations stack up in ways that are hard to assess: tiling approximations, Gaussian base shape, single-compartment neuron, simulation at very low firing probability (µF = 0.1) with extrapolation to spike trains, degree-8 polynomial fits to ηκ, and affine/polynomial fits in κ that the authors themselves note become unreliable for κ > 130; sensitivity to these choices is not systematically analyzed.

The scope and impact for a top-tier AI venue are modest: this is a fairly niche computational neuroscience contribution with no learning, AI systems, or methodological component likely to interest the broader community, and the main novel machinery (energy constraint ∫p(s)g(s)^α ds = E with α fixed to 1 by simulation) reduces to a relatively simple constant-gain solution in the infomax case.

Some technical details are under-justified: the choice I_conv = 1 in App. A, the equating of tuning curve widening with gain reduction via gsyn rescaling (App. H.2), and the energy budget mapping E(κ) = a1·ϵopt + a2 (eq. 16) whose fitted parameters are purely simulation-derived and never compared to measured physiological ATP rates.

strengths: The paper addresses an interesting and underexplored question: how energy budgets and firing rate homeostasis jointly shape optimal population codes, motivated by recent empirical findings of tuning curve flattening under caloric deprivation (Padamsey et al.).

The analytical framework is reasonably elegant: the tiling-based formulation with a generalized energy constraint (alpha exponent) cleanly recovers prior models (Ganguli & Simoncelli; Wang et al.) as special cases (alpha=1 and alpha=3/2), providing a unifying perspective, with a useful proposition showing approximate homeostasis emerges as a signature of optimality in prior frameworks.

The attempt to ground model parameters in a biophysically realistic NEURON simulation (including ATP accounting beyond spike counts, covering synaptic and leak currents) is a worthwhile effort to connect information theory to cellular physiology.

The paper includes fairly complete mathematical derivations (Fisher information approximation, homeostasis approximation, Lagrangian solutions for infomax/discrimax/Lp objectives) and reports a detailed simulation pipeline.
weaknesses: The central empirical validation is weak and arguably circular: the model's success on the mouse data of [22] is achieved by fitting free parameters (a1, a2 in eq. 16, i.e., the ratio a2/(a1*eps_ctr)=0.19625) specifically to reproduce the reported 32% widening and 29% ATP reduction. There is no out-of-sample prediction, no held-out dataset, and no quantitative fit comparison beyond a single example tuning curve. The claim that the method 'uniquely captures' the empirical behavior rests entirely on this single post-hoc parameter fit.

The headline result of perfect homeostasis (0% change in mean firing rate in Fig. 4b/e) is largely tautological: the approximate homeostasis constraint (eq. 5) is enforced exactly in the infomax/uniform-prior setting, so exact homeostasis is guaranteed by construction rather than being an emergent, falsifiable prediction.

The comparison to baseline models appears somewhat contrived. The baselines [5, 30] are applied under modified or assumed parameter changes (e.g., reducing firing rate to match tuning curve peak, or a 24% coding capacity reduction chosen to produce 32% widening), making the 'violation of homeostasis' numbers (-24%, -32%) more an artifact of how the comparison was set up than an intrinsic failure of those models.

The biophysical grounding involves a long chain of heavily engineered fits: degree-8 polynomial fits to noise, degree-1 energy fits, degree-2 width fits, affine fits of a1/a2 in kappa, and degree 2/4/2 polynomial fits to b1/b2/eta0 — with the authors themselves noting the fits become unreliable for kappa > 130 and deviate as kappa decreases. This layered fitting pipeline raises concerns about robustness and whether the derived noise-energy trade-off (eqs. 18-19) is more than a flexible curve fit.

The simulation itself is highly simplified: a single-compartment neuron responding to a single input spike, with a heuristic dispersed-Poisson noise model approximated by a Gaussian (App. B derivation of Fisher information via moment matching is loose), a single arbitrary choice to set the tiling constant I_conv to 1, and a low-firing-probability regime (mu_F = 0.1) whose validity for cortical neurons in vivo is not established.

Since the simulation fixes alpha = 1, the energy constraint reduces exactly to the mean firing rate constraint of Ganguli & Simoncelli, which the paper itself criticizes as overly simple. The actual distinguishing content over prior work — particularly Wang et al. [31], which already modeled metabolic constraints on population codes — is then primarily the homeostasis constraint and the simulation-derived dispersion term, which feels incremental.

Scope is narrow: one-dimensional scalar stimulus, Gaussian base shapes, tiling approximation, conditionally independent neurons (no noise correlations), and only uniform and one natural-scene prior. The impact on perceptual discrimination behavior (which [22] also measured) is not tested, though the framework could in principle predict it.

Several technical details are under-justified: the choice of kappa range (90-150) and its biological interpretation, the exclusion of parameter triplets with firing probability outside [.2, .8], the phi=0.02 compensation factor in the tuning curve construction, and the mapping between stimulus-dependent synaptic conductance and the abstract gain/density functions.

Given the paper's strong claims of generalization and a 'united explanation,' the evaluation provides little quantitative evidence against alternatives (e.g., a simple homeostatic variant of existing frameworks with an added dispersion term might reproduce the same qualitative flattening), leaving the added value of the full machinery unclear.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated contribution: connecting ATP-based energy budgets and firing rate homeostasis to optimal population coding is a novel angle that existing FI-based frameworks (Ganguli & Simoncelli; Wang et al.) do not capture, and the paper convincingly argues why prior models predict only shortening or widening, not flattening.

The analytical framework is genuinely more general: Sections 3.3 and Appendices E/K show that previous energy/population-size/total-FI constraints are recovered as special cases (α=1, α=3/2), providing a unifying view rather than an ad hoc model.

The biophysical grounding is a real strength: the NEURON simulation ties model parameters (α, ηκ(E)) to measurable cell properties (vrest, gleak), yields a testable noise-energy trade-off (eqs. 16-19), and makes falsifiable predictions about patch-clamp measurements under food restriction.

The paper honestly delineates how it differs from empirical terminology (footnote 1 on widening vs. flattening), provides detailed derivations for all analytical results, and reports failure modes of its own fits (App. J, deviations for κ > 130).
The comparison in Section 5 is fair and quantitative: homeostatic violations of competing models (-24%, -32%) are computed under the same assumptions rather than qualitatively dismissed.
weaknesses: Validation rests essentially on a single empirical dataset (Padamsey et al. [22]), and the key consistency check involves post hoc fitting of free parameters (a2/(a1·ϵctr) = 0.19625) chosen to match the reported 32% widening and 29% ATP reduction, which weakens the strength of the 'prediction' claim and borders on circularity.

The match to homeostasis is partly by construction: the approximate homeostasis constraint (eq. 5) is imposed as a hard constraint, so 'our model exhibits perfect homeostasis' is expected rather than an emergent prediction, making the head-to-head comparison in Fig. 4 somewhat asymmetric in the model's favor.

Several strong simplifying assumptions limit generality: Gaussian base tuning curves, tiling approximation, scalar stimuli only, single-compartment neuron model, and a dispersed Poisson noise model derived via a Gaussian approximation of FI — the paper acknowledges these but the practical consequences (e.g., for sigmoid/Gabor tuning curves common in visual cortex) are unexplored.

The noise dispersion ηκ varies only between ~1.000 and ~1.05 in the simulations; it would strengthen the paper to demonstrate that empirically observed noise increases under metabolic stress are actually of this magnitude, connecting the simulation scale to the experimental data.
Significance for a general AI audience is moderate: the contribution is squarely computational-neuroscience theory; impact on the broader AI/ML community is plausible but indirect.

Minor clarity issues: heavy reliance on appendices for the core simulation methodology, notation overload (Tab. 4), and some fitting choices (e.g., degree-8 polynomial for noise, degree-1 for energy) are justified only briefly.

strengths: The paper introduces two novel, mathematically tractable constraints (approximate firing-rate homeostasis and a generalized energy budget ∫p(s)g(s)^α ds = E) that unify previous optimal coding frameworks: it recovers Ganguli & Simoncelli (2010) at α=1 with firing rate as the energy proxy, and Wang et al. (2016a) at α=3/2, providing a clean, general analytical solution family (infomax, discrimax, general Lp) via Lagrangian methods.

The biophysical grounding is a genuine strength: an energy-dependent dispersed Poisson noise model derived from a stochastic Hodgkin-Huxley simulation (10,000 trials per cell state) links ATP consumption directly to noise dispersion η_κ(E), going beyond the standard 'energy = spike rate' proxy and capturing the empirically observed dissociation between maintained firing rates and reduced energy use.

The framework uniquely predicts the tuning curve flattening reported in Padamsey et al. (2022) while previous models predict shortening (Ganguli & Simoncelli) or widening (Wang et al.) — a clear, interpretable empirical differentiator, supported by a log-likelihood comparison (Sec. M.3).

Robustness analyses are thorough for this type of paper: noise correlations (differential correlations, Sec. N), non-Gaussian (Gabor) tuning curves, non-uniform priors, and varying activity levels κ are all checked, with the flattening prediction remaining robust.
Good reproducibility: full simulation code, parameter tables, and detailed derivations in the appendix; the pipeline from cell parameters to analytical model parameters (α, η_κ) is well documented.
weaknesses: The empirical validation rests on a single dataset (Padamsey et al., 2022), and key parameters are calibrated to that data: a2/(a1·εctr) = 0.19625 is explicitly fitted so that the model reproduces the reported 32% widening and 29% ATP reduction. This creates a circularity concern — the 'perfect match' in Fig. 4b is partly a consequence of fitting, not an out-of-sample prediction. The paper would be substantially stronger with a second dataset or held-out prediction.

The claimed 'exact match' of the tuning curve under a uniform prior is largely an artifact of the approximate homeostasis constraint becoming exact in that setting; deviations under non-uniform priors and non-Gaussian base shapes, while small (<2%, <5%), are acknowledged only in the appendix rather than the main claims.

The analytical contribution, while elegant, is technically incremental: closed-form solutions via Lagrange multipliers on a tiling-approximated Fisher information follow standard machinery (Ganguli & Simoncelli 2010; Wang et al. 2012), and the main novelty is the choice of constraints rather than new optimization theory.

The biophysical simulation uses a single-compartment neuron with simplified energy accounting (e.g., one lumped leak channel, single-spike inputs extended to spike trains via strong independence and low-rate assumptions in eq. 77), and the fit of η_κ degrades noticeably at low activity levels (κ < 100), limiting generality.

Several model choices are pragmatic rather than principled (e.g., fixing R(s)=1 and E=6 to match a 35-degree control width; suppressing A_disc/A_gen constants; the 17-parameter noise fit), and sensitivity of the α=1 conclusion to these choices is not fully explored.

The testable predictions (relationships between resting potential and leak conductance across activity levels) remain unverified; the likelihood-based calibration method (Sec. M.2) is proposed but admittedly not validated for stability, so the framework's data-fitting capability is still unproven beyond qualitative comparison.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuinely underexplored question: how optimal population codes should adapt under changing metabolic (energy) budgets, connecting efficient-coding theory to recent electrophysiology (Padamsey et al., 2022).

The framework is technically clean: the generalized energy constraint (eq. 7) with exponent α recovers both Ganguli & Simoncelli (2010) (α=1) and Wang et al. (2016a) (α=3/2) as special cases, providing a unifying perspective, and closed-form solutions are derived for infomax, discrimax, and general Lp objectives.

The biophysical simulation (stochastic Hodgkin-Huxley in NEURON, ATP accounting across synaptic/Na+/leak currents) provides a mechanistic grounding for the abstract energy constraint and the energy-dependent dispersed Poisson noise term, which is more principled than firing-rate proxies used in prior work.

The authors go beyond the main text with substantial supplementary analyses: robustness to non-Gaussian tuning curves (Gabor), non-uniform priors, differential correlations, spike-train statistics derivations, and a likelihood-based comparison on the empirical data.
The writing is generally clear, assumptions are stated explicitly, and the tiling/smoothness approximations are consistent with standard practice in this literature.
weaknesses: The central empirical claim risks circularity. In Sec. 5, the parameters (a1, a2, i.e., the calibration of E against the control condition) are fit precisely so that the model reproduces the 32% widening and 29% ATP reduction reported in Padamsey et al. (2022); the model is then presented as 'consistent with data.' The 'perfect tuning curve match' in the infomax/uniform-prior case is essentially guaranteed by construction (the authors themselves note this), so Fig. 4 provides little independent predictive validation.

Validation rests on a single dataset (one study, averaged tuning curves from 29 vs. 32 cells, with no repeated trials per cell). The authors acknowledge the data limitations, but this means the key claim—'uniquely captures' the observed flattening under homeostasis—is supported by one qualitative comparison against only two baseline models.

The comparison to baselines involves discretionary choices: for Ganguli & Simoncelli (2010) the firing rate is reduced to match the tuning curve peak rather than applying their model as-is, and the homeostasis violations of baselines (−24%, −32%) follow partly from these choices. A fairer, pre-registered comparison protocol would strengthen the claim of uniqueness.

Key model parameters are heavily fitted artifacts of the simulation pipeline rather than derived quantities: a 17-parameter noise fit, degree-1 energy fit, degree-4 noise fit with exponential weighting, polynomial fits of fitting parameters as functions of κ, plus the fitted energy mapping E(κ)=a1(κ)ε_opt+a2(κ). The derivation of α=1 follows from these fitted forms, so the headline result inherits substantial fitting flexibility; sensitivity of conclusions to these choices is not analyzed.

The assumption that metabolic-stress adaptation is noise-energy optimal (eq. 15) is asserted rather than established; the authors concede in the Discussion that cell responses may not be information-theoretically optimal, which undercuts the normative framing of the central result.

The theory is built on strong approximations (tiling, Gaussian base shape, locally constant priors, independence), and while robustness checks exist, the exactness claims in the main text (e.g., 'exact match to spike count') overstate what the approximations support.

Some methodological details reduce reproducibility confidence: notation overload (R vs R(s) vs R_n, multiple uses of E), reliance on proprietary-style NEURON session files, and numerical optimization details (penalty relaxation, gradient descent with fixed step size) whose convergence is not guaranteed.

strengths: The paper makes a clear and novel contribution by connecting optimal population coding theory directly to cellular energy (ATP) consumption, addressing a genuine gap: prior constrained-coding models (Ganguli & Simoncelli 2010; Wang et al. 2016a,b) cannot explain the empirically observed flattening of tuning curves under metabolic stress while maintaining firing rate homeostasis (Padamsey et al., 2022).

The proposed energy and approximate-homeostasis constraints are shown to formally generalize existing frameworks (recovering Ganguli & Simoncelli at alpha=1 and Wang et al. at alpha=3/2), providing a unifying mathematical account and clear positioning relative to prior work (Sec. 3.3, Fig. 1, Tab. 2).

Analytical solutions are derived cleanly for multiple coding objectives (infomax, discrimax, general Lp error), with full derivations in the appendix, and the model is grounded in a stochastic Hodgkin-Huxley biophysical simulation that yields an energy-dependent dispersed Poisson noise model — a nice theory-plus-simulation combination.

The empirical consistency check is compelling at the qualitative level: the model reproduces the reported 32% tuning curve widening and 29% ATP reduction while preserving mean firing rate, whereas competing frameworks predict shortening or widening with 24-32% homeostatic violations.

Unusually thorough robustness analyses: the flattening prediction is shown to be robust to noise correlations (differential correlations, Sec. N), non-Gaussian tuning curve shapes (Gabor base, Sec. L.3), and non-uniform stimulus priors, with mean firing rate deviations remaining small (<2-5%).
Reproducibility is reasonably addressed via detailed simulation parameters (Tab. 3), fitting procedures, and stated supplemental code.
weaknesses: Validation against data is limited to a single dataset (Padamsey et al., 2022) with only two summary statistics (32% widening, 29% ATP reduction); fitting the two free parameters (a1/a2) to match exactly these two numbers is weak evidence of predictive power. No held-out predictions, no fit to the full shape of the empirical tuning curves, and the 'exact match' under uniform-prior infomax is essentially guaranteed by construction of the homeostasis constraint.

The model rests on a long chain of strong assumptions and heavy parametric fitting: tiling, smoothness, conditionally independent noise, Gaussian base shapes, a 17-parameter fit of the noise dispersion, polynomial fits of energy/width/noise, and affine fits in activity level kappa. Some apparent quantitative agreement may reflect this fitting flexibility rather than the optimality principle; sensitivity of conclusions to these choices is not fully quantified.

The biophysical grounding uses a single-compartment neuron; the paper itself acknowledges that more realistic (multi-compartment, network) dynamics, and the possibility that metabolic responses are not information-theoretically optimal, are unaddressed and could undermine the normative interpretation.

Several analytical results have limited content: under the infomax objective the optimal gain is a constant (g = E^{1/alpha}), so the population optimization reduces largely to the choice of constraint exponent; the degree of freedom that distinguishes predictions comes mainly from the imposed constraint form rather than the optimization itself.

The approximate homeostasis constraint is exact only under a uniform prior; its accuracy for general p(s) is justified only via a first-order approximation and post-hoc numerical checks, and the derived E = const interpretation of prior work (Prop. E.1) is elegant but of secondary significance.

Impact is specialized to computational neuroscience / efficient coding; while this is a legitimate NeurIPS-style topic, the paper does not offer methods or insights likely to transfer to broader AI audiences.

The likelihood-based model comparison (Sec. M) is underdeveloped: the authors themselves note the calibration method is unstable and that the data (averages over different cells from different animals) are not appropriate for a likelihood computed over repeated trials, so the reported log-likelihood ordering should be treated as illustrative at best.
